definition: Character encoding is a convention of using a numeric value to represent each character of a writing script.
details: Not only can a character set include natural language symbols, but it can also include codes that have meanings or functions outside of language, such as control characters and whitespace. Character encodings have also been defined for some constructed languages. When encoded, character data can be stored, transmitted, and transformed by a computer. The numerical values that make up a character encoding are known as code points and collectively comprise a code space or a code page. Early character encodings that originated with optical or electrical telegraphy and in early computers could only represent a subset of the characters used in languages, sometimes restricted to upper case letters, numerals and limited punctuation. Over time, encodings capable of representing more characters were created, such as ASCII, ISO/IEC 8859, and Unicode encodings such as UTF-8 and UTF-16. The most popular character encoding on the World Wide Web is UTF-8, which is used in 99.0% of surveyed web sites, as of September 2026. In application programs and operating system tasks, both UTF-8 and UTF-16 are popular options.

explainer.lead: Character encoding gives each character a numeric value so a computer can handle written text. Without this shared convention, storing, sending, and transforming characters would not work reliably.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a codebook that gives every letter or symbol its own number. A computer can save or send those numbers, then use the same codebook to turn them back into characters. Some codebooks also include numbers for spaces and special instructions, not just letters.
tiers.practitioner: Character encoding is applied whenever character data is stored, transmitted, or transformed. UTF-8 is the dominant choice on the web, while UTF-8 and UTF-16 are both popular in application programs and operating system tasks. A key limitation of older encodings is their restricted repertoire, sometimes covering only uppercase letters, numerals, and limited punctuation.
tiers.paperLevel: For a set of characters C, a character encoding is a convention that associates each character c in C with a numeric value called a code point. The code points collectively form a code space or code page, which may also include control characters and whitespace. Encodings differ in coverage: early systems represented only subsets of written language, whereas later systems such as ASCII, ISO/IEC 8859, UTF-8, and UTF-16 expanded representational capacity.

explainer.example: In a simple illustrative encoding, suppose the character A is assigned the code point 65. A computer can store or transmit 65 as the encoded form of A, and the same encoding convention identifies which character that value represents.

explainer.intuition: A character encoding is like a shared numbering scheme for written symbols. Once characters have numbers, computers can work with the numbers while people continue to work with readable text.
howItWorks: Choose an encoding that defines which characters and other codes it covers.
Associate each character with a numeric value called a code point.
Treat the complete collection of code points as the encoding's code space or code page.
Use the encoded values to store, transmit, or transform character data.
Select an encoding with enough coverage for the symbols the task requires.
explainer.whyItMatters: Encoding turns writing into data that computers can store, transmit, and transform. Broader encodings also overcome the severe character limits of early systems, supporting more letters, punctuation, whitespace, and control functions.
misconceptions: Character sets are not limited to natural-language letters: they can also contain control characters and whitespace.
A code point is one numeric value, while a code space or code page is the collective set of those values.
Not every encoding can represent every character; early encodings sometimes supported only uppercase letters, numerals, and limited punctuation.
